act: the twisted-horned stag leaps about together with the young doe in the rain-fed millet
sense: the beasts of the season are already together, as the husband and wife will be when the chariot that passes them arrives

note: Nakkirar gives each of the six faces and the twelve hands a work in the world; Arunagirinathar asks to hold the same faces, arms, feet, vel and peacock in thought every day.
teaches: The list of the god's faces and arms began as a description of what he does for the world and became, in the later hymn, a sequence to meditate on, so the same inventory moved from cosmology to devotional practice.

note: The sages who have cast out lust and fierce anger walk first into Avinankudi; the Siddhar poet clears lust, anger and the great lie out of his heart so that it can become the Lord's bedchamber.
teaches: Driving out lust and anger is in the idyll the qualification of a class of sages to approach the god's shrine, and in the later poem the housework every devotee must do to make the heart itself the shrine.

note: The idyll's assembly of gods comes with Brahma 'in mind' and a need it does not name; the Thiruppugazh number-poem tells that Murugan imprisoned Brahma and freed him when the three gods came begging at his feet.
teaches: If the Thiruppugazh's story is the one behind lines 160 to 165, the oldest Murugan poem already assumes the episode of Brahma's imprisonment, and the later hymn only states outright what the idyll leaves as an allusion.

note: Nakkirar's Eragam is the shrine where brahmins recite the rare six-letter mantra; Arunagirinathar's Eragam is where 'the brahmins of the six letters' (ஆறெழுத்து அந்தணர்) praise his feet.
teaches: The six-letter brahmins of Eragam pass from Nakkirar's description into Arunagirinathar's epithet almost word for word, showing that the later poet read the shrine through this idyll's line 186.

note: Nakkirar defines the brahmins of Eragam by their outward order (six duties, three fires, sacred thread, wet cloth, chanting at set hours); Tirumular defines the true brahmins by meditating on the mantra and riding the chariot of love so as not to sink in maya.
teaches: The same figure of the mantra-reciting brahmin is praised by the idyll for keeping the forms and by Tirumular only for the inner love the forms should lead to, which shows the Saiva yogic tradition re-grounding a figure it inherited.

note: In the idyll, dancing on every hill with the hill women is the god's settled nature (குன்றுதொறாடலும் நின்றதன் பண்பே); in the Thiruppugazh, Kunruthoradal is the name of a shrine where the hill tribes worship him with frenzied dance (வெறியாடி).
teaches: A phrase that in the Sangam idyll describes the god's habit among the hill people became by Arunagirinathar's time the proper name of a shrine, so the idyll's description is the origin of a later place of pilgrimage.

note: The idyll finds the god in every outer place of worship, festival ground, veri ground, grove, river, crossroads and kadamba tree; Sivavakkiyar asks what use any puja is while the Lord being sought is within us. On the reading that the Siddhar rejects outer places and rites altogether, the two are incompatible.
teaches: The idyll widens the god's presence outward to every spot where he is called, and the Siddhar narrows it to the one place inside the worshipper, so the pair marks the two ends of the Tamil argument over where the divine is met.
audit_text_issue: the sense of siddhar line 1-2 is tentative

note: The idyll's rite offers rice mixed with a ram's blood and spreads millet with blood, and calls it worship that brings each seeker what he sought; Tirumular says that in worship the bright flower is not killing other small lives. Read plainly, one counts a killing as part of right worship and the other counts not killing as the best offering.
teaches: Blood offering stands in the oldest Murugan poem as an ordinary part of effective worship, so Tirumular's rule that not killing is the true flower is a reform of an existing Tamil practice, not a restatement of it.

note: The idyll says those who worship with offerings of goat's blood and red millet obtain what they ask; Sivavakkiyar says that offering goat and cock at the shrine when you are sick does not stop you wasting away. The claims about whether such offerings work are incompatible.
teaches: The Siddhar's mockery of goat and cock sacrifice is aimed at a rite the Sangam idyll describes in detail and promises results from, so his scepticism attacks a claim with a long and respected Tamil history.
audit_text_issue: the sense of siddhar நங்கச்சொல்லு and மூஞ்சூராய் is uncertain

note: Nakkirar calls the god 'bull among poets of praised good speech' (புலவர் ஏறே); the Thiruppugazh says Murugan delighted in the poems of Keeran (Nakkirar) and taught him grammar.
teaches: The idyll's epithet makes the god a poet, and the later tradition turns that into a story in which the idyll's own author becomes the god's pupil, so the poem's praise of the god's speech came back as the poet's legend.

note: The seeker says it is hard for living beings to know the god to his measure (நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின்); Tirumular says Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, measuring with thought, cannot conceive the Lord, who stands beyond all measuring.
teaches: The theme that the god cannot be measured, which Tirumular argues through the gods' failure, is already in the Sangam idyll as the suppliant's reason for coming to the feet, so unknowability led to approach rather than to despair from the start.

note: In the idyll the god appears in his own form to a living suppliant and says 'Fear not; I knew of your coming'; in the Thiruppugazh the poet asks that at the moment Death's servants come he appear on the peacock and end his fear.
teaches: The god's appearance and his word against fear, which the idyll promises to any suppliant who makes the journey, the later poet saves for the single hour of death, showing how the guide-poem's promise of a meeting became a plea for rescue.

note: The Kural likens the wealth of a man of நயன் to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town; the guide says he went to Karikalan like a bird that thinks of a fruiting tree, through a gate that bars no one in need.
teaches: The Kural states the tree from the giver's side and makes its public place the point, while the idyll shows the same tree from the hungry bird's side and supplies the condition the couplet compresses into உள்ளூர், an open gate, so the maxim's promise turns out to depend on access as much as on fruit.

note: Puram 209 compares the bard to birds that fly to a fruit tree in a mountain cleft and turn back with nothing when it is bare; the guide uses the bird and fruit tree as the image of certain success.
teaches: The bird-and-fruit-tree simile carried the bard's risk as well as his hope, since in Puram 209 the tree can be bare, so the guide poem's use of it is a claim that this patron is never the empty tree, and its first-person testimony is offered to meet exactly that doubt.

note: Puram 140 mocks the lord of Nanjil as a simpleton who gave an elephant when asked for a little rice, giving that knows no measure; here Karikalan gives elephants with mates and calves by the measure he knows, and the bard takes by the measure he knows.
teaches: The elephant given to a bard was a stock sign of excessive giving that one poet could tease as folly ignoring measure, while the idyll answers that charge by naming two measures, the giver's and the taker's, so the excess is kept in bounds by the receiver's restraint.

note: The idyll makes the battle of Venni, where two great kings fell on one field, the crown of Karikalan's praise; Puram 66, addressed to Karikalan himself, says the king who was wounded in the back at Venni and starved himself facing north is the better man.
teaches: The same victory at Venni is in one poem the proof of Karikalan's greatness and in the other the occasion for saying the loser surpassed him, which shows that praise addressed to a victor could, in this poetry, rank the defeated king's honour above the win itself.

note: In Puram 385 the lord of Ambar, hearing a bard's drum at another man's door, strips off his earth-eaten rags, dresses him in white and ends his hunger; the guide promises that Karikalan will strip off the bard's stitched rags and give him silk before he asks.
teaches: Puram 385 tells the removal of rags and the gift of cloth as one patron's spontaneous kindness, while the guide poem can predict it as the first step of a known sequence, which suggests the re-dressing of the bard was a recognised rite of reception rather than a single generous act.

note: Naladiyar 2 tells those who gain wealth to share its food with many at once, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; the idyll's bard passes on to others what he received on the road, and the king, weighing the instability of the world, will not dismiss his guest.
teaches: The impermanence that the Naladiyar uses as an argument for giving is already in the idyll a motive at both ends of the gift, the bard redistributing as he goes and the king holding on to the guest, so instability argued for keeping company as well as for releasing wealth before it became a quatrain about wealth alone.

note: Puram 7 praises Karikalan for delighting in plunder by the light of burning enemy towns, so that the good things are gone from others' rich lands of fields and fish; the idyll shows his own land as one umbrella under which all five landscapes mingle in plenty.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the same Chola fertility, fields where water and fish abound, as what Karikalan destroys in other kings' lands and what he guarantees in his own, so the guide poem's harmony of the five lands is the domestic face of a conquest the puram poet praises openly.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the idyll grants that in Karikalan's land, under a sceptre it has just called just, the rain can fail in great drought, and gives the harvest to the Kaveri instead.
teaches: On the idyll's reading the just king's land is not spared drought, which the Kural's couplet implies it should be, so the poet keeps the king's righteousness and the land's plenty together by moving the source of harvest from the sky, which answers to the sceptre, to the river, which does not need to.

note: Puram 117 says that even when Saturn smokes, comets appear and Venus runs south, the rain never failed in the dry land of the just king; the idyll describes a sun that makes kings tremble, falls that dwindle and clouds that forget the sea, and sets the Kaveri against them.
teaches: Both poems meet the same fear, that signs in the sky foretell drought and blame the king, but Puram 117 denies that the rain fails in a good king's land while the idyll admits the failure and lets the river make it harmless, two different ways of protecting a ruler's name from a bad season.

note: The guide here calls the bard he directs முதுவாய் இரவல (line 40); in Thirumurugatruppadai line 284 the god's attendants announce the devotee to Murugan in the same words, முதுவாய் இரவலன்.
teaches: The same title for a seasoned suppliant names a bard seeking a chief in one guide poem and a devotee seeking the god in another, so the devotional guide poem approached Murugan through the bard's petition at a patron's gate and kept even its form of address.

note: Both describe Kuttuvan's western land by a buffalo that leaves the lotus pond to rest in jackfruit shade; Akananuru 91 says the hero will not stay for it even if he gains it, and the idyll calls even Kuttuvan's Vanji empty.
teaches: The buffalo resting in the jackfruit shade was a set emblem of the Chera land's ease, and both genres used it as the standard of plenty that is outweighed: by the heroine's beauty in the love poem and by a minor chief's giving in the guide poem.

note: Both name the seven givers (Pari, Ori, Kaari or Malaiyan, Athikan or Ezhini, Pekan, Aay, Nalli), with the shared formula for Pekan's hill guarded by a fearsome god (அருந்திறல் அணங்கின் / அருந்திறல் கடவுள்) and the same closing என ஆங்கு எழுவர.
teaches: The seven were a fixed list with stock epithets that a poet could set before a living patron, and the two poems use it differently: Perunchithiranar says the seven are dead so Kumanan must take their place, while the idyll says Nalliyakkodan already bears alone the yoke the seven bore together.

note: Avvai praises Athiyaman for giving her the nelli fruit without saying what it would do for him; the idyll lists Athikan as the giver of the nectar-yielding fruit to Avvai.
teaches: Avvai's poem makes the hiddenness of the fruit's virtue the point of the gift, whereas the idyll names that virtue openly (அமிழ்துவிளை), so by the time the story joined the list of seven the secret had become its public meaning.

note: Paranar cites Pekan's gift of a cloak to a peacock as proof that his giving looks to others' need and not to merit in the next world; the idyll lists the same gift as Pekan's emblem among the seven.
teaches: In Purananuru 141 the peacock's cloak is evidence in an argument about why a chief gives, while in the idyll it is only the sign by which Pekan is recognised, so a deed that once carried a claim about motive could circulate as a bare token of liberality.

note: Both show a bard's hunger by a mushroom growing in a cold kitchen (ஆம்பி) and a starving woman and her children; Perunthalai Saathanar shows it to Kumanan as his present state, the idyll's guide as a past state the patron ended.
teaches: The same kitchen of poverty serves as a petition in the Purananuru poem and as testimony in the guide poem, which shows how the guide form works: the bard's own former misery, once relieved, becomes the credential that sends another bard to the same patron.

note: The Kural says a ruler easy to see and not harsh of speech has his land praised above others; the idyll praises a gate never shut to bards, poets and brahmins, a glad face and freedom from fierce anger, each praised by a named class of people.
teaches: The Kural's abstract reward of praise has a concrete source in the idyll, where the people at the open gate (wise men, warriors, women and suppliants) are the ones who do the praising, so accessibility is rewarded by the very classes it admits.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbending sceptre; the bard's song praises both, the sceptre that shades the ploughmen and the spear that burns the chariot warriors.
teaches: The bard gives sceptre and spear equal places by assigning them to different people, subjects and enemies, while the Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear even in war, so the ethical book turns the praise poem's balanced pair into a hierarchy.

note: The idyll's bards wander like birds that search for fruiting trees on a hill the rain has left; the Kural likens the wealth of a man with nayan to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: The patron-as-fruit-tree image is seen from the tree's side in the Kural and from the birds' side in the idyll, and the idyll adds the condition the Kural's town tree removes: the guide poem exists because, for the wandering bard, the fruiting tree is far off and must be pointed out.

note: Both address a ragged bard with a small lute; Purananuru 138 sums up the road he has already crossed in three lines (cattle paths, deer hills, fish fords), and the idyll lays out the road still ahead land by land.
teaches: The guide poem's landscape sequence appears in the short poem as a compressed formula for the journey behind the bard; the idyll turns it round into the journey before him and expands each land into a settlement with its own meal.

note: In Purananuru 141 a bard resting on the road with his gifts tells a hungry bard that before seeing Pekan they were poorer than he; the idyll's speaker, with horses and elephants, says he and his hungry kin come from Thiraiyan.
teaches: The meeting of a rewarded bard and a hungry one is the whole drama of the short poem but only the opening frame of the idyll, which shows that the long guide poem grew by keeping that encounter and filling the space between it and the patron with the road.

note: The idyll says Thiraiyan is of the line the waves brought (திரைதரு மரபு); Akananuru 340, a shore poem, likens the girl to his Pavaththiri of many flowering seaside groves.
teaches: Read together, the two place Thiraiyan as a ruler of the coast: the praise poem's sea-born lineage and the love poem's choice of his seaside town as the measure of a neythal girl's beauty rest on the same identity, so the akam simile draws on the fame the guide poem states.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll says that in the land of Thiraiyan's just sceptre robbers are absent and thunder, snakes and beasts do no harm.
teaches: The idyll extends the Kural's claim that a just ruler's land is blessed by nature from rain and crops to the dangers of the road, so for a travelling bard the just sceptre is proved by a safe journey rather than a good harvest.

note: Both use the formula of the salt carts that proclaim their rate (கொள்ளை சாற்றி, கொடுநுக ஒழுகை); in Akananuru 159 raiding bowmen cook meat at the cold hearths the salt carters left, on the road the lover crossed.
teaches: The same stock road scene serves opposite ends: in the love poem the salt-carters' track is where raiders lurk and the woman fears for her man, while in the guide poem it is a road made safe for travellers by day under the patron, so the formula's meaning is set by whose land the road runs through.

note: The idyll's warriors trade raided cattle for toddy and drink home brew all day as part of a life of valour; the Kural forbids drink, allowing it only to those who do not wish to be counted by the worthy.
teaches: The Kural's ironic concession names a class of people who do not seek the esteem of the worthy, and the idyll shows that such a class was a whole warrior community whose honour lay in the raid, not in sobriety, so the Kural's ban addresses a scale of values the older poem did not share.

note: The idyll's herd girl buys food with buttermilk (அளை) but will not take gold for ghee; in Kalittokai 110 the herd girl rebukes a man who thinks one easy to buy buttermilk from is easy for butter too.
teaches: The Kalittokai girl's retort turns on a real price difference that the idyll records, buttermilk as cheap daily barter and ghee as a good kept for livestock, so her wordplay about being 'easy' depends on the herding economy the guide poem describes.

note: The Kural says only those who live by their own ploughing truly live and all others bow to eat and follow behind; the idyll's bard, who lives by praise, is fed millet and beans at the farmers' village.
teaches: The idyll shows the arrangement the Kural ranks: the bard is exactly one who eats from another's plough, yet the guide poem treats being fed by farmers as the patron's honour and the bard's due, not as a lesser life, so the Kural's verdict is a moral claim against the old patronage order.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies; the idyll describes a town that has never known hunger, whose granaries grow old unopened and whose children sleep fed on milk.
teaches: What the Kural defines by absences the idyll shows by presences (unopened granaries, toy chariots, nurses, white rice and fowl for a guest), and its phrase தொல்பசி அறியா makes freedom from hunger a property of the town's history, not only of its present.

note: The Kural says the base, like sugarcane, yield only when crushed; the idyll's cane presses roar day and night and the bard is told to drink the juice as he likes.
teaches: The Kural's image of giving extracted by force uses the same press that the idyll presents as the very sound of open plenty, so the simile's sting depends on the contrast: what the base give only under crushing, the cane in a good land gives to any passing guest.

note: The guide promises the bards rice toddy brewed by fisherfolk and roasted fish until they stagger; the couplet says do not drink, or let only those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy drink.
teaches: The idyll counts drinking to the point of staggering among the best hospitality of the road, given freely by the poorest folk, while the couplet makes drink the mark of one who forfeits esteem, so the ethics book is rejecting a pleasure the oldest praise poetry offered as part of the gift.

note: Both praise a wife as chaste like the northern star: here the Brahmin wife who cooks for the bards, in Purananuru 122 Kari's wife, the one thing he keeps while all else goes to Brahmins and bards.
teaches: In both poems the star-chaste wife stands at the centre of a house that gives to Brahmins and bards, but in the chief's poem she is what is kept back from giving and in the idyll she is the one who gives, so the simile marked the giving household from either side.

note: In the idyll a kingfisher strikes a bathing girl's golden earring for a fish and carries it off to a sacrificial pillar; in the Naladiyar quatrain a kingfisher takes the beloved's eyes for carp but does not dive, seeing her brow as a drawn bow.
teaches: The kingfisher's mistake about a woman's ornament or feature was a set conceit: the idyll lets the bird act on its mistake as part of a port scene, while the later love quatrain stops the bird short, turning the same error into praise of the woman's brow.

note: The toddy-sellers keep a boar in a pit for many days, fed on rice flour and kept from its sow, to serve its fat to the bards; the couplet says that if no one killed to eat, no one would bring flesh for sale.
teaches: The idyll describes exactly the chain the couplet condemns, an animal fattened in confinement to be served and sold, and offers it as a reward of the road, so the Kural's argument against buying meat cuts against a hospitality the guide poems praise.

note: The Paripadal hymn makes the god lying in waking sleep on the many-hooded serpent in the milk sea one of his three cosmic forms; the idyll places the one on the serpent bed at a grove shrine on the road where bards stop to praise him and play a little.
teaches: Together they show the serpent-bed form both as cosmic theology and as the god of a particular shrine on the road to Kanchi, so in the Sangam period the same image was already tied to local worship that a passing bard could visit.

note: The Paripadal fragment likens Madurai to the lotus from Mayon's navel, its streets the petals and the lord's palace the pericarp; the idyll has Kanchi's tall-housed town rise like the pericarp of the lotus from the blue god's navel that bore the four-faced one.
teaches: The navel-lotus with the central great house as its pericarp was a shared figure of city praise used for Kanchi as well as Madurai, so it was a convention for a Tamil capital rather than a legend of one city.

note: Purananuru 2 praises a Chera for feeding the armies without limit while the hundred fought the Five until they fell; the idyll uses the same war to say its king roared at his victory like the Five when all the hundred fell.
teaches: The pair shows two ways Sangam praise borrowed the Bharata war: the Chera poem keeps its king outside the war as the feeder of both sides, while the Tondai idyll puts its king in the victors' place, so the epic could measure a king's giving or his conquest.

note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

note: Purananuru 185, by Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan himself, says the realm is a cart that runs well only if its driver is skilled and otherwise sinks in the mire of enmity; the idyll shows the same king's court running smoothly, justice and gifts granted to all.
teaches: Read beside the patron's own conditional maxim, the bard's portrait answers the king's worry with a finished picture: what Ilanthiraiyan states as a risk depending on the driver, the guide poem states as already achieved, which shows the work praise did for a king who wrote about failure.

note: The guide scripts the bard's praise of the patron (warrior of warriors, lord of the wealthy, of unceasing giving) as the way to his gifts; Arunagirinathar confesses that praising people as lotus-handed and clouds in giving, to beg from them, wounded his heart, and asks to serve Murugan instead.
teaches: The patron praise that the guide poem teaches as a craft with a sure reward is in the later hymn the very habit the poet repents, so the bard's profession that founded Tamil praise poetry became for the devotional poet the model of misplaced service.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai has a flesh-eating demoness dance the thunangai after the god kills Sur; here the bard's praise is likened to the finger-snapping before the goddess of the thunangai, mother of the one who killed Sur in the sea.
teaches: Both guide poems use the Sur victory and its thunangai dance, but the god's guide poem uses it to praise the god while the king's guide poem makes it the model for praising a man, so the form of Murugan's praise was lent to the praise of a patron.

note: Weighing the condition of the unlasting world, the king gives before the bard has finished asking; the couplet says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts.
teaches: The idyll turns the couplet's 'at once' into a patron's habit with its motive stated, wealth that will not stay given for fame that will, so the maxim had a heroic model in the bard's patron before it became a rule of the ethics book.
audit_text_issue: line 467 first letter restored (யந்நிலை) from an older e-text

note: Both strip the suppliant's rag like old pond moss, dress him in new cloth and feed him meat and rice; Purananuru 390 ends by saying that kings with elephants do not even know such feeding.
teaches: The rag, cloth and meal follow a fixed order of the gift rite in both, and holding them together shows the idyll claiming for a crowned king the very hospitality that Purananuru 390 boasts only the lesser chief gives, so the boast was rhetoric and not a rule of rank.

note: Purananuru 361's patron gives golden lotuses to bards and garlands to the singing women and needs no one to tell him the world does not last; the idyll's king crowns the bard with a golden lotus and garlands the viraliyar after weighing the unlasting world (line 466).
teaches: Placed together, the golden lotus for the bard and the garland for the singing woman appear as a fixed pair of gifts tied to one stated motive, the patron's knowledge that the world does not last, which lets the Purananuru king face Death and makes the idyll's king hurry the gift.

note: Both idylls have women reassure the waiting wife with the words இன்னே வருகுவர் (they will come soon), and both have her refuse it in tears: காட்டவுங் காட்டவுங் காணாள் கலுழ்சிறந்து here, உகத்தவை மொழியவும் ஒல்லாள் மிகக்கலுழ்ந்து in Nedunalvadai.
teaches: The promise of a quick return and the wife's weeping refusal form one fixed sequence in both idylls, but Mullaippattu takes the promise from a herd-girl's words to a calf, read as an omen, while Nedunalvadai puts it in the grey-haired nurses' mouths as plain comfort, so the convention let the same words come from chance speech or from household authority, and in both the comfort must fail.

note: Kar Narpathu 12 says the dark clouds rising every day on the right (வைகலு மேரும் வலம்) are a sign beyond doubt (ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி) that he will come; Mullaippattu opens with a cloud that drinks the sea and rises on the right (வலனேர்பு).
teaches: Read with Kar Narpathu's explicit rule that a cloud rising on the right foretells the lover's return, Mullaippattu's opening simile is already an omen in the sky set before the old women's omen in the street, and the poem closes with the returning army also rising on the right (line 91), so the idyll is framed by the sign and its fulfilment.

note: In Akananuru 9 the returning husband pictures his wife at the evening when calves come home, standing at a corner of the house and praying at every chirp of the lizard; in Mullaippattu the old women seek the omen at evening, a calf supplies it, and the wife will not accept it.
teaches: The husband's picture of a wife eagerly reading every omen is his own fancy on the road; Mullaippattu, told from the house, gives the omen-seeking to the old women and shows the wife refusing its comfort, which qualifies the hopeful, praying wife of the man's imagination.

note: Purananuru 22 praises the king under whose umbrella the unarmed sleep safe (வாள் மருங்கு இலோர் காப்பு உறங்க) because he himself does not sleep (நீ துஞ்சாய் மாறே); Mullaippattu sets armed women, old guards, hour-keepers, Yavanas and Mlecchas round the king's own bed at midnight.
teaches: The praise of a wakeful king who lets others sleep safely has a reverse side that only the idyll shows: the king's own sleep needs a whole household of armed and foreign watchers, so royal protection of the realm's sleep rests on others guarding his.

note: Mullaippattu's king lies awake thinking of the maimed tusker, the fallen men and the arrow-struck horses; Nedunalvadai's king goes out at midnight with a lamp-bearer to see his soldiers' wounds (விழுப்புண் காணிய புறம்போந்து) and does not sleep (பள்ளி கொள்ளான்).
teaches: The two idylls give the same scene of a king kept awake in camp by his wounded, as inward thought lying with a hand on the bed in Mullaippattu and as an outward round of inspection in Nedunalvadai, and only Mullaippattu lets the night end in the sweet sleep (இன்துயில்) that the wife at home is denied.

note: Kural 780: a death that fills the eyes of those who maintained one with tears is worth begging for; Mullaippattu's king remembers those who fell having made good the rice they ate (சோறுவாய்த் தொழிந்தோர் உள்ளியும்).
teaches: The Kural measures the warrior's best death by the tears of the one who fed him, and the idyll shows that patron from inside, lying awake over the men who repaid his rice with their lives, so the maxim gains a scene where the debt of food and the king's grief are both seen.

note: Akananuru 214: in the rain-drowned camp the king, set on glory, has no sleep (கண்படை இலனே), and the soldier wonders how his wife fares alone in the rainy evening; Mullaippattu 67: the king, eager for battle, gets no sleep (கண்படை பெறாஅ), and the next lines turn to the wife.
teaches: Akananuru 214 compresses the idyll's two scenes, the sleepless king in the rainy camp and the wife alone at evening, but splits king and husband into two men, which shows that Mullaippattu's joining of them, the wife's husband being the sleepless king himself, is the idyll's choice and not the convention's rule.

note: In Kar Narpathu 8 the kaayaa opens buds as if dipped in the eye's collyrium (கண்ணிய லஞ்சனங் தோய்ந்தபோற் காயாவும்) and so announces his return; in Mullaippattu 93 the kaayaa blooms collyrium (காயா வஞ்சன மலர) on the road his chariot is driving.
teaches: The collyrium-dark kaayaa is a promise in Kar Narpathu, pointed to by the friend while the man is away, and in the idyll it is scenery the returning chariot passes, so the same flower serves as proof of the return in the short poem and as the return itself in the long one.

note: Mullaippattu 85 lights the wife's room with பாவை விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல; Nedunalvadai 175 lights the king's midnight round of the wounded with பாண்டில் விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல.
teaches: The same half-line of a lamp's thick flame burning lights the sleepless wife at home in Mullaippattu and the sleepless king in camp in Nedunalvadai, so the formula belongs to the night vigil itself and the two idylls assign that vigil in opposite directions.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll opens on a world where the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and credits it to the rule of the patron's ancestors among truthful men.
teaches: The idyll gives the Kural's cause-and-effect rule a cosmic setting and a past: the plenty is the order of the world itself and belongs to the ancestors' rule, so a king inherits a moral weather he must keep up rather than earning it afresh, which is what the counsel later in the poem asks of him.

note: The same poet praises the same king for the battlefield sacrifice: in Purananuru 26 with crowned heads for a hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in the idyll with the arm as ladle and the flesh-rice served to the soldiers who did not step back.
teaches: Mangudi Maruthanar's two accounts of the rite show what it was for: the short poem sets it beside the king's Vedic sacrifices as a second, martial sacrifice, while the idyll names who eats it, the soldiers who held their ground, so the horror is also the army's feast and reward.

note: The idyll gives the victory at Alankanam as its patron's crowning deed (camping fearsomely, killing kings, taking their drums); in Akananuru 209 the friend says the gossip about the heroine is louder than the roar at Alankanam when Chezhiyan beat the seven.
teaches: Held together, the two show the battle the court poet offers as the king's defining glory already serving an akam poet as a proverbial measure of noise for village gossip, so a royal victory entered the common stock of comparison and was expected to be known to every hearer.

note: Kalladanar tells the same king that he has seen the ruin of the enemy's land, ending on a doe with her fawn, her stag killed by a tiger, nibbling velai flowers in a manless waste; the idyll lists, line by line, each human use of the enemy's land replaced by a wild one, with the owl and its mate in the fallen mansions and the boar and its sow in the ploughed fields.
teaches: Both poets of this king measure conquest by animal couples moving into places emptied of human families, so the ravaged-land description had a fixed device; the idyll turns Kalladanar's single pathetic image into a systematic inversion of the land's uses, which is the material its kaanchi counsel will later weigh.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because some would not eat even Indra's nectar alone; the idyll says the king would not leave true friendship for a lie even if he gained the high world with its nectar.
teaches: The 'even for the gods' nectar' test appears in both, but Purananuru 182 uses it for sharing among anonymous worthies while the idyll uses it for a king's truthfulness to his friends, so the virtues that hold the world together were also demanded of the ruler, and the measure for them was the same.

note: The Kural rates the worst poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; the idyll says the king, offered the treasure Vanan buried in the south, would not say 'let blame come to us', but would rather give treasure away for fame.
teaches: The idyll shows the Kural's maxim as a king's test with a named treasure and adds the alternative the Kural leaves out, giving wealth away for fame, so refusing blamed gain is tied to giving: the ruler's honour lies in both refusing and spending.

note: Mangudi Kizhar ends Purananuru 24 by saying that the only ones who truly lived are those who, born in the wide world, did not pass with the many but stayed in fame; in the idyll he says the kings who ruled the wide world with their fame spreading are more than the sand on the shore, and are gone.
teaches: The same poet who told this king that fame alone outlasts death here counts the famous kings by the grains of sand, so fame does not exempt anyone from passing and is itself common; the counsel of the idyll is harder than the short poem's consolation, and the pair shows the kaanchi argument being sharpened by its own author.

note: The idyll counts the noise of the garlanded crowd playing together on cool Parankunram among the sounds of the marutham countryside; Paripadal 17 describes the crowds revelling between song-rich Koodal and Parankunram, garlanded men and women dancing so that the bees cannot reach the flowers.
teaches: In the Maduraikkanchi the Parankunram festival is one sound among the reaping drum and the herons, part of the king's agrarian land, while the Paripadal makes the same crowd its subject and the hill's beauty, so the festival a court poet counted as rural plenty became, in the devotional songs, the sign of the god's hill.

note: The idyll's sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring balance; the Kural says the vast sea itself would lose its nature if the cloud took and did not give back.
teaches: The sea's unchanging fullness was a stock figure of plenty in the city poem, and the Kural takes the same sea to show that the fullness depends on the return, which, read back into the market, makes Madurai's inexhaustible plenty the effect of continual exchange rather than a fixed store.

note: The idyll's அந்தணர் are marked by Veda, rite and high conduct, and only in passing by a loving heart; the Kural says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous because they are kind to every creature.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Kural keeping the idyll's name but moving its definition from the Veda and the rite to the one trait the idyll mentions last, kindness, so the couplet reads as a deliberate redefinition of a status the court poem took for granted.

note: Purananuru 6 wishes the Pandya Mudukudumi to lean to no side like the beam of a balance (ஞமன்); the idyll gives the same balance (ஞெமன்கோல்) to Madurai's court of justice, which puts away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
teaches: The impartiality that the earlier poem asks of the king in person has, in Nedunjeliyan's Madurai, become the work of an institution, and the idyll spells out the five passions the court must set aside, which the wish to the king left unnamed.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:6 line 9 ஞமன்ன் has a doubled final consonant, probably a misprint for ஞமன்.

note: The Kural's worthy man is like the balance that first levels itself and then weighs; the idyll's court is straight like the balance once it has put away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
teaches: The idyll's list says what the Kural's 'first making itself level' consists of, the clearing of five named passions before judgment, so the couplet's compressed image can be unpacked from a description of a working court.

note: The idyll names the courtesans' many deceiving lies and hidden embraces and their draining of rich young men, but lists them among the splendours of the city; the Kural likens the false embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
teaches: The deceit the Kural turns into horror was already admitted, in the same terms of lying and false embrace, by the court poet, who still counted it as part of the city's wealth, so the moralist's chapter answers a practice that praise poetry had treated as a sign of prosperity.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veri ground and the festivals of every town among the places where Murugan is found; the idyll shows the velan and a priestess at work in Madurai's squares, serving pregnant women, with kurinji and kadamba worn in the city.
teaches: The guide poem gives the rite's places and the city poem gives its users, so together they show the hill god's veri carried into the capital and used for women's life crises such as pregnancy, which neither poem states alone.

note: Kalladanar shows Nedunjeliyan's work in enemy country: fouled fords, plundered fields, felled guarded trees, burned houses, an empty waste; the idyll shows tuskers, horses and herds brought by the light of burning towns flowing into Madurai like the Ganges into the sea.
teaches: The two poems are the two ends of one process under the same king: the ruin praised in the Purananuru is the source of the abundance praised in Maduraikkanchi, so the city's splendour is the enemy land's emptiness moved to the capital.

note: The Kural says many will live by a king who looks at people not alike but by rank (வரிசை); the idyll's king crowns warriors with the gold thumbai 'not asking who they are' but weighing their order (முறைகருதுபு), after listing the deeds that rank them.
teaches: The idyll shows a ceremony in which the king's ranking goes by deeds rather than by birth, which supports reading the Kural's வரிசை as an order of merit and shows what the couplet's 'many will live looking to it' meant in practice for a warrior following.

note: In Purananuru 72 Nedunjeliyan stakes his vow on the poverty of not giving to suppliants; the idyll shows his gate never barred, bards, singers and poets called in, and chariots and elephants given.
teaches: Read together, the open-gate scene is the vow's condition kept: what the young king named as the shame he would accept if he failed (not being able to give) is what the poet, in the king's own lifetime, presents as his settled daily practice.

note: Purananuru 15 addresses Mudukudumi himself, asking whether his enemies or his completed Vedic sacrifices are more; the idyll measures Nedunjeliyan's feast against one shared with the teachers trained in the sacrifices of Mudukudumi of many halls.
teaches: The sacrifices that Purananuru 15 praises as one king's deeds had become, by Nedunjeliyan's time, an inherited institution with its own line of teachers, and the standard against which a later Pandya's liberality was measured.

note: Nedunjeliyan vows that if he fails, poets with Mangudi Maruthan at their head may cease to sing his land; the idyll, by Mangudi Maruthanar, ends with chiefs with Maran at their head praising him in assembly.
teaches: The vow names the poet whose song was at stake, and the idyll is that poet's song, ending in a praise-assembly built on the same 'X at the head' formula, so the pair shows the poet answering the king's vow in kind while closing, as kaanchi, on the bound of the king's good time.

note: Purananuru 6 ends by wishing Mudukudumi to last on earth like the cool moon and the burning sun; the idyll uses the same pair to show Nedunjeliyan shining among his kin, then closes on the good time he has been given within a bound.
teaches: The kaanchi poet takes the dynasty's formula of sun and moon but uses it for brightness among kin, not for duration, and pointedly ends on the limit of the span, so the closing withholds exactly the wish for lastingness that the praise poem gave.

note: Naladiyar 6 starts from the appointed span of days and concludes: give your wealth away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; the idyll starts from the good time given within a bound and concludes: rejoice and live sweetly every day.
teaches: Both counsels rest on the same premise of a fixed span, but the idyll, after showing the king's giving, lets pleasure stand beside it as a right answer, while the ethics book allows only giving, so the later text narrows a kaanchi argument that once had room for enjoyment.

note: Both open the cold season with white musundai, kodal and cowherds coming in from the rain with wet garlands, and both close the description with the same words, கூதிர்நின் றன்றால் followed by பொழுதே (here போதே, line 72).
teaches: In Akananuru 264 the formula hands the season to a waiting woman who asks whether the men in the king's camp know their own state, so the idyll's cold-season opening, which ends on the same words, reads as that akam season-poem expanded, with its closing camp scene as the answer to her question.

note: In both idylls the waiting wife is told இன்னே வருகுவர் and still weeps; in Mullaippattu the words are an omen overheard from a herd girl to her calves, in Nedunalvadai they are the foster mothers' practised comfort.
teaches: Mullaippattu's promise is a sign that its poem fulfils with the returning chariot, while Nedunalvadai's is only kind speech that its poem never fulfils, so the same words separate a poem of waiting rewarded from one that can end only in the poet's wish.

note: The queen gazes at a painted moon with Rohini and sighs; Akananuru 136 sets a wedding at the hour when the moon had joined Sakatam, the Rohini asterism, in a spotless conjunction.
teaches: Since weddings were timed to the moon's union with Rohini, the painting over the queen's bed is also the sign under which she was married, so her long sigh can be read as memory of her own wedding as well as envy of a pair never parted.

note: The Kural counts every day without a glorious wound (விழுப்புண்) as wasted; the idyll's king walks the camp at midnight in the rain to see the glorious wounds (விழுப்புண்) of the warriors who felled elephants.
teaches: The Kural makes the wound a soldier's private reckoning of his days, and the idyll shows its public side, the king coming out at night to look at each wound, so the honour the soldier counts by was conferred in person by his king's seeing it.

note: In both a king in a rain-soaked camp will not sleep (கண்படை இலனே; பள்ளி கொள்ளான்); in Akananuru the soldier cites it to tell his heart the war is his duty while she hears the evening alone, in Nedunalvadai the poet sets it beside the queen's grief and prays for the war's end.
teaches: The king's sleepless diligence is the soldier's reason for staying away in the Akananuru and the poet's ground for hoping the war ends soon in the idyll, so one camp image can either lengthen the separation or promise its end, depending on whose grief frames it.

note: Mullaippattu's king lies sleepless in his tent thinking of elephants wounded by spears and of men who fell repaying their food; Nedunalvadai's king rises and goes out at midnight to see his wounded.
teaches: The two camp kings show one care in two forms, remembered in bed in Mullaippattu and acted out by walking the lines in Nedunalvadai, so the night-time thought for the wounded is a fixed mark of the good war king in these idylls, the more vivid of them putting it into motion.

note: Yavanas make the lamp-figures that light the queen's inner chambers in Nedunalvadai; in Mullaippattu fierce armed Yavanas guard the king's tent.
teaches: Read together, the idylls place Yavanas at both ends of a royal household, as craftsmen inside the women's palace and as bodyguards in the war camp, so the king trusted these foreigners with the light of his queen's rooms and with his own person.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that the mother's velan rite, held for a sickness read as Murugan's seizure, will expose the secret; in the idyll the mother's diviners and offerings to many gods have already failed, and the friend makes that failure the ground for telling her.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the misread sickness and its useless rite are the hinge of the kurinji plot: the short poem stops at the girl's dread of exposure, and Kapilar's idyll starts from the same point and turns the failed cure into the friend's reason to disclose the love and press for marriage.

note: The Kural likens those fallen from their station to hair fallen from the head; the friend says broken jewels can be rejoined but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages.
teaches: The friend uses the Kural's idea that a fall in standing is beyond repair as an argument for speaking at once, not for keeping quiet: because a girl's good name cannot be restored once it is lost, the secret has to come out before gossip costs her it, so the maxim on honour drives the plot of disclosure.

note: Kovur Kizhar stands between two Chola kings at war and tells them that whichever loses, their own house loses; the friend says she holds two great fears like the worthy who stand between two great kings bent on war.
teaches: Purananuru 45 shows from inside the position the idyll's simile names, the mediator who can win nothing for either side: so the friend's double fear, for the father's honour and for the girl's life, is modelled on the puram envoy's predicament, and the akam go-between borrows the role of the poet who speaks between kings.

note: Both are told by the friend to the mother in disclosure: in Akananuru 48 a garlanded hunter with a bow asks the girls which way the beast went; in the idyll the hunter says he has lost a beast that came this way and, when they keep silent, asks whether even speaking with him is a blame.
teaches: Read together, the hunter's question about a lost beast stands out as the conventional opening of the hill meeting reported in அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், and the idyll supplies what the short poem leaves to the mother's wit: the girls' silence out of fear of blame and the man's answer to that fear.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai places Murugan at the veri ground and under the fresh-flowered kadamba; the idyll compares the terrified girls holding hands to the ring of women possessed by Neduvel dancing round a kadamba trunk.
teaches: The possession dance that Thirumurugatruppadai describes as worship is used by Kapilar as the image for the girls at the very moment the love begins, so the god-seizure the mother wrongly suspects in the opening lines comes back as a simile for what really happened.

note: Both poems by Kapilar have toddy made by ripe jackfruit in a long rock pool (பாறை நெடுஞ்சுனை, விளைந்த தேறல்) drunk unknowingly by a creature: a monkey that cannot climb and sleeps, a peacock that staggers like a rope-dancer.
teaches: The same poet uses one formula for two jobs: in Akananuru 2 the drunk monkey is an argument that the lover can easily find the joy he plans, while in the idyll the drunk peacock only praises the plenty of the lover's land, which shows that in Kapilar the image's force depends on where it stands in the speech, not on the image itself.

note: The Kural says household life and its guarding of goods exist to care for guests; the man's oath promises a house of open doors where he and the girl will eat what is left after feeding guests.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the household exists for guests is already in the idyll the language in which a hill man pledges marriage: what he swears to give the girl is not a feeling but a guest-feeding house, so the ethic of virundhu was the content of the promise before it was a maxim.

note: Akananuru 122 lists the hindrances that keep the lover away (the sleepless town, the mother, guards who hurry, the dog, the moon); the idyll lists nearly the same (guards hurrying, the fierce dog, the mother waking, the moon) as what turns him back every night.
teaches: In Akananuru 122 the girl uses the catalogue of hindrances to complain about their secret love, whereas the friend in the idyll gives it to the mother as proof of the man's constancy, since he goes back each time without anger, so the same list can work as a lament or as a testimonial depending on who is listening.

note: In Akananuru 112 the friend tells the man who has come at night of the bear and the tiger on his path and asks why he does not marry; the idyll ends with the girl weeping over the tiger, bear, elephant, crocodiles and spirits of his night path, told to the mother.
teaches: The dangers of the night path press for marriage from both sides: in Akananuru 112 they are told to the man to make him propose, and in the idyll to the mother to make the family consent, so the same catalogue is used as leverage on whichever party is holding back.

note: The Kural says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the whole wide world; the idyll says that though the sky fails, the Kaveri does not, and the Chola fields never stop yielding. On the literal reading the claims conflict: the Kural admits no land exempt from failed rain, the idyll names one.
teaches: Read together they show that the Kural's universal law of rain met a regional boast in the poets' own geography, a river delta praised precisely as the place the warning does not reach, although the idyll's own line 6 (மலைத்தலைய) concedes that the river too begins as rain on the hills.

note: The Kural names customs (உல்கு) as one of the three kinds of the king's wealth; the idyll shows Puhar's customs men levying duty every day without shortfall and stamping the tiger seal on goods for the good king.
teaches: The Kural's single word for customs revenue is in the idyll a working institution with officers, a royal seal and a daily round at the port, so the couplet's category can be seen to name an administration the earlier poets had watched in operation.

note: The Kural says a trader's true trade is to care for others' goods as his own; the idyll's merchants weigh their own goods and others' alike (தமவும் பிறவு மொப்ப நாடி) and take no more and give no less.
teaches: The idyll's phrase is nearly the Kural's பிறவும் தமபோல், and it adds the working test of fair dealing at the scale, so the maxim appears first as the praised reputation of a real merchant class in a named port before it is stated as a rule for all traders.

note: The Kural argues that if no one killed to eat, no one would sell meat; the idyll praises a city where killing is banned and beasts crowd safely at the meat-sellers' huts, yet the same city fries fish and flesh in its toddy-shop yards (lines 176-177) and its fishermen eat prawns and tortoise (lines 63-64).
teaches: Held together they show the ban on killing in the older poem as the virtue of particular classes in a city that still ate meat, whereas the Kural's demand-side argument makes every buyer answerable, so the later ethic is stricter than the ideal the idyll praised.

note: In Akananuru 213 the friend assures the heroine that the man will not linger abroad even if he were given the world of the gods with its nectar (அமிழ்தொடு பெறினும்); in the idyll the man himself says he will not leave her even if he were given the city (பட்டினம் பெறினும்).
teaches: The 'even if he were given' formula is in the Akananuru a friend's comfort about a man already gone; Pattinappalai puts it in the man's own mouth before he leaves and spends 217 lines making the offered prize a real city, one it has itself likened to heaven (line 104), so a convention of comfort becomes the frame of a whole idyll.

note: In Akananuru 123 the man in the desert mocks his heart, which can neither cross the hills for wealth nor stay with her without fearing poverty; the Pattinappalai hero tells his heart he will stay with her though the richest city is offered. On the reading that both answer the same choice between wealth and love, the first treats staying as fear of poverty and the second as the right decision.
teaches: Paalai poets argued both sides of the same debate with the heart, and the pair shows that giving up the journey (செலவழுங்குதல்) was a recognised, honourable answer to the very reproach Akananuru 123 makes, not only a failure of nerve.

note: Karunkuzhal Athanar tells Karikalan to his face that his delight in plunder by the light of burning towns makes the good lands of others cease to be; the idyll describes the same king's wasting of enemy fields and halls as glory and then uses it to measure the heat of the desert.
teaches: The same king's ravaging of fertile land could be addressed to him as a praise with a sting (நல்ல இல்ல ஆகுபவால்) or listed without reserve in a long court praise, so the pair shows how much the frame, a short puram address or an akam idyll, decided whether a poet could let the cost of conquest be heard.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai names the common, the public hall and the place with the sacred post (மன்றமும் பொதியிலும் கந்துடை நிலையினும்) among the places where the god is worshipped; the idyll shows such a hall with its post (கந்துடைப் பொதியில்), once lit with lamps and worshipped by many, now a lodging for a wild elephant and its cow.
teaches: The pair shows that the hall with the sacred post was a standing institution of town worship in both poems, and that wasting an enemy country meant emptying exactly these places of worship, so the idyll's picture of conquest is measured against the ordinary religious life the Murugan poem describes.

note: Venni Kuyathiyar praises Karikal's victory but says the king he defeated at Venni, who sat facing north to die ashamed of a wound on his back, is better than he; the idyll's catalogue of the peoples Karikalan crushed has no such voice, and praises his men for never turning their backs (ஒருவேமெனப் புறக்கொடாது).
teaches: Both poems turn on the shame of the turned back, but the short puram poem lets a woman poet rank the defeated king's honour above the victor's, while the long praise gives the ethic only to the victor's side, so the pair shows what the conquest catalogue had no room to say.
audit_text_issue: Line 290 is a repaired reading (ஒருவேனெப் to ஒருவேமெனப்), and whose men lines 289 to 291 describe is not certain.

note: The Kural says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; the idyll gives Karikalan both, the spear hot to his enemies and the sceptre cool to his people, and uses them as the measures of the forest's heat and the heroine's coolness.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear as the source of victory, while the idyll keeps the two as equal faces of one king, each true in its own sphere, so the pair shows the rhyme வேல் and கோல் as an older fixed figure of kingship that the Kural argued with and the akam poet borrowed for love.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the veri ground the velan prepares (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among the god's dwellings, with village festivals and hill places; the idyll sets mansion women at their windows joining hands to red Murugan and crowding with the veri dancers in Puhar's festival bazaar.
teaches: The veri rite, which the Murugan poem places in the hills and the village grounds, appears in Pattinappalai in a port city's bazaar among the mansions, so the pair shows the possession rite of the hills carried into urban festival life by the time of the idyll.

note: Both guide poems describe the bard's lute part by part, and both lay its leather cover like the line of soft hair on a woman's belly (மயிர் ஒழுகிய); Porunaratruppadai's woman is newly pregnant, Malaipadukadam's a bride whose hair still smells of the wedding.
teaches: The hair-line simile for the lute's cover recurs, with the same verb, in two idylls by different poets, so it was a fixed part of the bards' description of their own instrument, and each poet varied only the stage of the woman's life.

note: The idyll says Nannan brings back treasures from those whose backs he has seen and pours his gifts on poets (சுரக்கும், 71-72) and lays waste the enemy front (முனைபாழ், 59); Akananuru 349, in a heroine's lament, names a Nannan who lays waste the front, breaks forts and pours their wealth unasked (சூழாது சுரக்கும்) on bards who come with their kin.
teaches: An akam heroine can name Nannan's land by a two-line formula that the guide poem unfolds into a whole promise to a troupe, which shows the patron's praise circulated as a fixed epithet that love poets could assume their hearers knew, though the identity of the two Nannans is not certain.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts at a host's changed face; in the idyll the hill people take the troupe in as kin without asking who they are and speak sweet words to end the loneliness of a far country, but only after the troupe says it is the Vel's musicians.
teaches: The idyll confirms the Kural's point that a welcome lies in the manner more than the meal, but it shows the welcome opened by the patron's name rather than owed to any guest, so in the guide poem hospitality is a sign of a king's reach, not the householder's duty the Kural makes it.

note: Purananuru 281 calls a friend to guard a warrior's wound with lute, mustard, incense and the singing of kaanchi; Malaipadukadam hears among the hill's sounds the song hill women sing as a guard (காப்பு) to soothe the tiger-torn wounds on their husbands' chests.
teaches: The rite of guarding a wound with song, which the Purananuru gives to a hero hurt in the king's war, appears in the idyll as an ordinary household sound of the hill after a hunting injury, so the puram poem's rite drew on a common practice of protection rather than one reserved for battle.

note: Perunthalai Sathanar says the wealthy who gave nothing to the needy are not remembered, while those who set up fame are; in the idyll the patron counts the enthroned rich whose names died with them as more than river sand and decides that his days shall pass with fame.
teaches: The argument a bard uses in Purananuru 165 to shame and urge patrons appears in the idyll as the patron's own reasoning, so the guide poem shows the bards' doctrine of fame taken in by the giver as his motive for giving.
audit_text_issue: Malaipadukadam 552 இலமென மலர்ந்த கையர் admits two readings

note: The Kural says nothing stands undying in the world but towering fame; the idyll sets beside the patron's choice of fame a crowd of dead rich men past counting whose names went with them.
teaches: The Kural states that fame alone survives without saying what the alternative looks like; the idyll supplies it as a number, the sands of a riverbank, so the couplet's single survivor is measured against a vast forgetting.

note: The Kural says giving without the misery of saying 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born; the patron, hailed as the scion of an unfailing line, will not let the bards even finish telling of their journey before he welcomes them.
teaches: One of the senses of the couplet, giving before the asker must speak of his need, is in the idyll a court scene in which the patron cuts short the suppliants' account, and the idyll ties it, as the Kural does, to the giver's lineage.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; in the idyll everyone in the patron's town looks on the arriving bards sweetly and gladly before any gift is given.
teaches: The Kural makes the host's face the guest's first need inside one household; the idyll extends that glad look to a whole town, so the welcoming face becomes a public mark of the patron's realm rather than a private courtesy.

note: The guide tells the bards to enter Nannan's heavily guarded gate without hesitation; Purananuru 151 tells a kinsman of Nannan of the golden chariot that the poet's people have shunned his hill because of a door shut against singers.
teaches: If both poems speak of one house, the open guarded gate the idyll promises is the standard by which Perunthalai Sathanar shames the kinsman: a lineage's fame for an open door becomes a claim its heirs can fail.

note: In the idyll the forest men who have broken a hard stronghold (அருங்குறும் பெறிந்த) set aside their spoil as guest-tribute for their lord; in Akananuru 349 Nannan pours out unasked to weary bards the great wealth taken from broken strongholds (அருங்குறும்பு எறிந்த).
teaches: Read together the two poems show a chain of wealth: the spoil of forts taken by the hill people goes to Nannan as tribute and goes out again from him to the bards, so the patron's generosity praised in love poetry rests on his people's raids.

note: On the road, stones stand at the forks bearing the names of undying fame (செல்லா நல்லிசைப் பெயரொடு) of warriors who gave their lives; at court the patron reflects that rich men who did not give died taking their names with them.
teaches: The idyll makes one argument across the road and the court: a name survives on the stone of the man who gave his life or in the fame of the man who gives his wealth, and is lost with the man who gives nothing.
